notes: Help page dat.assink2016 (metadat 1.6-0), examples: res <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/esid), then moderators one at a time (pubstatus, year, deltype releveled to general) and rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ year + deltype, random = ~ 1 | study/esid), filed here; the intercept-only fit is its simplification, and the later fits with a vcalc V matrix (rho = 0.6, or 0.7 and 0.5 by deltype) keep the grouping. 100 standardized mean differences (yi) of recidivism in juveniles with and without a mental health disorder, from 17 studies. esid numbers the effects within study, so study:esid has one level per row: its term is effect-level and stays in the formula, its column goes to ignore with the row id id. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance vi, which the formula leaves out. Source: Assink & Wibbelink (2016), TQMP 12(3), a three-level meta-analysis tutorial.

Help page dat.bakdash2021, examples: res.overall <- rma.mv(es.z, vi.z, mods = ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | SampleID / Outcome, test = 't') and res.sa <- rma.mv(es.z, vi.z, mods = ~ 0 + SA.measure.type, random = ~ 1 | SampleID / Outcome, test = 't'), filed here (res.overall is its simplification); the alternative parameterization random = ~ factor(Outcome) | factor(SampleID) has the same grouping. 678 z-transformed correlations of situation awareness with task performance (ghost results imputed) from 79 studies (SampleID) of 77 papers. Outcome is unique per effect, so its term is effect-level and its column goes to ignore; Author, Title, DOI and DTIC.link label the paper. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance vi.z (from Sample.size.stats), which the formula leaves out. Bakdash et al. (2021), Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science.

RULE GAP: an arm-based network meta-analysis table whose page fits only netmeta. Help page dat.baker2009, examples: pw <- pairwise(treatment, exac, total, studlab = paste(study, year), sm = 'OR'); net <- netmeta(pw, common = FALSE, ref = 'plac'), a random-effects network meta-analysis on the pairwise log odds ratios, and the additive component model netcomb(net); neither is a mixed model on this table, so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's arm-based binomial GLMM with a trial intercept. 94 arms (one row per arm) of 39 COPD trials (id, labeled by study and year); exac counts patients with one or more exacerbations out of total. Baker, Baker & Coleman (2009).

Help page dat.begg1989, examples (after dat$trt <- relevel(factor(dat$trt), ref='CMO') and dat$arms <- relevel(factor(dat$arms), ref='2')): the Begg & Pilote (1991) model rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ trt, random = ~ 1 | study, method='ML') and, filed here, the model with bias terms for the uncontrolled studies rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ trt + trt:arms, random = ~ 1 | study, method='ML'); two variants add a random treatment effect, random = list(~ 1 | study, ~ trt | study) with struct='UN', tau2=c(0,NA), rho=0 (an extra BMT-arm variance) or struct='CS', on the same grouping. 20 two-year disease-free survival rates (yi, a proportion) of bone-marrow transplantation (BMT) or chemotherapy (CMO) from 16 studies: 4 controlled studies give both arms, 12 are single-arm. The source weights each rate by its sampling variance vi (sei its root), which the formula leaves out. Begg & Pilote (1991), Biometrics.

Help page dat.berkey1998, examples: V <- vcalc(vi=1, cluster=author, rvars=c(v1i, v2i)); rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, random = ~ outcome | trial, struct='UN') and, filed here, rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome + outcome:I(year - 1983), random = ~ outcome | trial, struct='UN', method='ML'). Multivariate meta-analysis: 5 trials each give the mean difference (surgical vs non-surgical) in probing depth (PD) and attachment level (AL); the unstructured random effect per outcome is the correlated slope outcome|trial. author labels the trial. The source weights the effects by their known 2x2 sampling covariance (v1i, v2i; vi the variances), which the formula leaves out. Berkey et al. (1998), Statistics in Medicine.

formula: (1 - 3 / (4 * (exp_n + con_n) - 9)) * (exp_mean - con_mean) / sqrt(((exp_n - 1) * exp_n * exp_se^2 + (con_n - 1) * con_n * con_se^2) / (exp_n + con_n - 2)) ~ 1 + (1 | study_ID) + (1 | comp_ID)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size. Help page dat.besson2016, examples: dat$sd_c <- con_se * sqrt(con_n); dat$sd_e <- exp_se * sqrt(exp_n); escalc(measure='SMD', m1i=exp_mean, m2i=con_mean, sd1i=sd_e, sd2i=sd_c, n1i=exp_n, n2i=con_n); mod1 <- rma.mv(yi ~ 1, V = vi, random = list(~ 1 | study_ID, ~ 1 | comp_ID)). The response names escalc's first input (the experimental group's mean), the formula's left side is the standardized mean difference (Hedges' g, its correction factor approximated) as an expression of the columns, and response_type is the effect size's; confidence is medium for that reason only. 473 comparisons of offspring behaviour (anxiety, exploration, activity) after maternal diet manipulation in rodents, from 55 studies (study_ID); comp_ID is unique per row, so its term is effect-level. dam_ID and animal_ID index dam and offspring groups the model does not fit, con_ID shared controls. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Besson et al. (2016).

formula: log((waward / (wtotal - waward)) / (maward / (mtotal - maward))) ~ type + (1 | study) + (1 | study:obs)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size. Help page dat.bornmann2007, examples: escalc(measure='OR', ai=waward, n1i=wtotal, ci=maward, n2i=mtotal); res <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/obs) and, filed here, rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ type, random = ~ 1 | study/obs) (fellowship vs grant applications). The response names escalc's first input (women awarded), the formula's left side is the log odds ratio of an award for women vs men as an expression of the columns (escalc adds 1/2 only to tables with a zero cell), and response_type is the effect size's; confidence is medium for that reason only. 66 award comparisons from 21 studies; obs numbers them within study, so study:obs has one level per row and its term is effect-level. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Bornmann, Mutz & Daniel (2007), Journal of Informetrics.

RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size. Help page dat.bourassa1996, examples: escalc(measure='OR', ai=lh.le, bi=lh.re, ci=rh.le, di=rh.re, add=1/2, to='all'); rma(yi, vi, subset=sex=='combined'); rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/sample, subset=sex=='combined'); then the page keeps a sample's male and female rows where both are reported and its combined row otherwise and fits, filed here, rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/sample/sex) (a subset fit filed on the whole object: the 96 rows hold one combined row for each of the 54 samples and 21 male/female pairs). The response names escalc's first input (left-handed left-eyed), the formula's left side is the log odds ratio of handedness and eye dominance with the 1/2 correction, and response_type is the effect size's; confidence is medium for that reason only. Sample numbers are unique across the 47 studies; study:sample:sex has one level per row, so sex goes to ignore and its term stays in the formula. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Bourassa, McManus & Bryden (1996), Laterality.

Help page dat.cohen1981, examples: escalc(measure='ZCOR', ri=ri, ni=ni); rma(yi, vi), a random-effects model with one effect per row and no study level, so published_model is no. 20 correlations of course instructor ratings with student achievement; study labels repeat (16 studies, Centra 1977 and others give one correlation per course type, sample), so study is the grouping factor by the ruling on repeated clusters, inferred from the column, hence low. The rma heterogeneity term has no column (no row id). The source weights each effect by its sampling variance 1/(ni - 3), which the formula leaves out. Cohen (1981), via Cooper & Hedges (1994), Appendix A.

formula: ri ~ 0 + interaction(var1, var2) + (0 + interaction(var1, var2) | study)
notes: RULE GAP: the random term is an unstructured effect per correlation (the var1.var2 pair) within study, which random_slopes cannot name since the pair is no single covariate; the formula carries it and random_slopes stays blank, hence medium. Help page dat.craft2003, examples: tmp <- rcalc(ri ~ var1 + var2 | study, ni=ni) builds the var1.var2 pair and the sampling covariance V of the raw correlations; rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + var1.var2, random = ~ var1.var2 | study, struct='UN'). Multivariate meta-analysis of the 6 correlations among CSAI-2 cognitive anxiety (acog), somatic anxiety (asom), self-confidence (conf) and sport performance (perf) in 10 studies (studies 6 and 17 give a subset). The source weights the effects by V (from ni), which the formula leaves out. Craft et al. (2003), via Becker & Aloe (2019).

Help page dat.crede2010, examples: escalc(measure='ZCOR', ri=ri, ni=ni); rma(yi, vi) per criterion with moderators class and year; multilevel: rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | studyid/sampleid, subset=criterion=='grade') and the same with subset=criterion=='gpa', filed on the whole object with the two subsets named here. 97 correlations of class attendance with class grade or GPA from 88 samples in 68 studies; within each subset studyid:sampleid has one level per row, so its term is effect-level and sampleid goes to ignore (9 samples report both criteria). The source weights each effect by its sampling variance 1/(ni - 3), which the formula leaves out. Crede, Roch & Kieszczynka (2010), personal communication to metadat.

RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size; the response names escalc's first input (the elevated-CO2 mean plant mass) and the formula's left side is the log ratio of means. Help page dat.curtis1998, examples: escalc(measure='ROM', m1i=m1i, sd1i=sd1i, n1i=n1i, m2i=m2i, sd2i=sd2i, n2i=n2i); rma(yi, vi, method='DL') and the same on the subsets xtrt=='FERT' & level=='LOW' and xtrt=='LIGHT' & level=='LOW': a random-effects model with one effect per row and no paper level, so published_model is no. 102 observations (id) of woody plant mass under elevated vs ambient CO2 from 29 papers that vary further treatments (xtrt, level), so paper is the grouping factor by the ruling on repeated clusters; the documentation numbers papers and observations, hence medium. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Hedges, Gurevitch & Curtis (1999), Ecology.

formula: (1 - 3 / (4 * (nt + nc) - 9)) * (mt - mc) / sqrt(((nt - 1) * sdt^2 + (nc - 1) * sdc^2) / (nt + nc - 2)) ~ 0 + outcome + (1 | study)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size, and the long table mixes continuous outcomes (rnic1, rnic2, snic1, snic2: means and SDs) with binary ones (rngoal1, rngoal2, sngoal1, sngoal2: xt and xc of nt and nc). Help page dat.dagostino1998, examples: escalc SMD from mt, mc, sdt, sdc, nt, nc and escalc OR from xt, xc, nt, nc; rma(yi, vi) per outcome (one row per study each); V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=study, obs=esid, rho=0.7) and rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, subset=outcome %in% c('rnic1','rnic2')) with no random effects (no noteworthy heterogeneity), so published_model is no. The filed row is the reader's: the standardized mean difference (Hedges' g, correction approximated; the response names its first input mt) per continuous outcome with a study intercept, the binary outcomes' rows leaving it missing. 72 rows, 8 outcomes per antihistamine trial (9 studies). The source weights each effect by its sampling (co)variance, which the formula leaves out. D'Agostino et al. (1998).

Help page dat.demir2022, examples: escalc(measure='ABT', ai=alpha, ni=n, mi=items), Bonett's transformation -log(1 - alpha); rma(yi, vi), one effect per row and no study level, so published_model is no. 33 Cronbach's alphas of the Mother-to-Infant Bonding Scale (esid, one per row) from 26 studies (studyid, up to 4 each), so studyid is the grouping factor by the ruling on repeated clusters; the documentation names study and effect size ids, hence medium. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance (from n and items), which the formula leaves out. Demir et al. (2022), a reliability generalization meta-analysis.

RULE GAP: an arm-based network meta-analysis table whose page fits only netmeta. Help page dat.dogliotti2014, examples: pw <- pairwise(treat = treatment, n = total, event = stroke, studlab = study, sm = 'OR'); net <- netmeta(pw, ref = 'plac') and the Mantel-Haenszel netmetabin(pw, ref = 'plac'); neither is a mixed model on this table, so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's arm-based binomial GLMM with a trial intercept. One row per arm of antithrombotic trials in non-valvular atrial fibrillation (id, labeled by study), strokes out of total. Dogliotti, Paolasso & Giugliano (2014).

RULE GAP: an arm-based network meta-analysis table whose page fits only netmeta. Help page dat.dong2013, examples: pw <- pairwise(treatment, death, randomized, studlab = id, sm = 'OR'); net <- netmetabin(pw, ref = 'plac'), a Mantel-Haenszel common-effect network meta-analysis, with netsplit for inconsistency; no mixed model on this table, so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's arm-based binomial GLMM with a trial intercept. 99 arms of trials of inhaled COPD medications (id), deaths out of randomized. Dong et al. (2013).

RULE GAP: an arm-based network meta-analysis table whose page fits only netmeta. Help page dat.gurusamy2011, examples: pw <- pairwise(treatment, death, n, studlab = study, sm = 'OR'); net.MH <- netmetabin(pw, ref = 'cont') and net.IV <- netmeta(pw, ref = 'cont'); no mixed model on this table, so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's arm-based binomial GLMM with a trial intercept. One row per arm of trials of interventions to decrease blood loss in liver transplantation, deaths at 60 days out of n; the details note one study with zero events in both arms that every network analysis drops. Gurusamy et al. (2011), via Efthimiou et al. (2019).

Help page dat.hasselblad1998, examples: escalc(measure='PLO', xi=xi, ni=ni, add=1/2, to='all') per arm; arm-based network meta-analysis with fixed study effects rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + factor(study) + trt, random = ~ trt | study, rho=1/2, btt='trt'), filed here (compound symmetry with the correlation fixed at 1/2, named in this note); the later contrast-based models run on a to.wide restructure, not this table. 50 arms (id) of 24 smoking-cessation studies comparing no contact, self-help, individual and group counseling; xi abstinent out of ni. study is both a fixed effect and the grouping factor, so the grouping stands and factor(study) stays in the formula only. The source fits the normal approximation of the arm log odds, weighted by their sampling variances, which the formula leaves out. Hasselblad (1998), Medical Decision Making.

Help page dat.huber2000: individual participant data, one row per patient (601) of five randomized placebo-controlled studies of OM-89 (Uro-Vaxom) in recurrent urinary tract infection. The examples compute a Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney statistic per study (wilcox.test of recurrences by treatment) and its common-language effect size, and fit no model, so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's Poisson GLMM with a study intercept; the design is documented, hence medium. Huber et al. (2000).

formula: yi ~ 0 + outcome + outcome:I(log(hrs) - mean(log(hrs), na.rm = TRUE)) + (0 + outcome | study)
notes: Help page dat.kalaian1996, examples: V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=study, type=outcome, rho=0.66); rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, random = ~ outcome | study, struct='UN'), then, filed here, mods = ~ 0 + outcome + outcome:loghrs with loghrs = log(hrs) - mean(log(hrs), na.rm=TRUE); a last variant fixes tau2=c(NA,0) for the verbal outcome. 67 standardized mean differences of coached vs uncoached SAT scores (verbal or math; id one per row) from 47 studies; the unstructured random effect per outcome is the correlated slope outcome|study. The source weights the effects by V, which the formula leaves out. Kalaian & Raudenbush (1996), Psychological Methods.

Help page dat.knapp2017, examples: rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/comp); V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=study, grp1=group1, grp2=group2, w1=n_sz, w2=n_hc, obs=task.diff, rho=R); rma.mv(yi, V, random = ~ 1 | study/comp) and, filed here, rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ difficulty, random = ~ 1 | study/comp), with robust inference clustered by study. 66 standardized mean differences in planning performance of schizophrenia patients vs healthy controls from 31 studies; comp numbers the comparisons within study, so study:comp has one level per row and its term is effect-level. yi_iq and vi_iq are the IQ effect sizes, an alternate response. The source weights the effects by V, which the formula leaves out. Knapp et al. (2017).

Help page dat.konstantopoulos2011, examples: rma(yi, vi); rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study); res.ml <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | district/school), filed here; the multivariate parameterization random = ~ school | district has the same grouping. 56 standardized mean differences of achievement under a modified vs a traditional school calendar, one per school, schools within 11 districts (school codes restart within district). RULE GAP: this pass's brief renders ~ 1 | district/school as district;school, but district:school has one level per row (study is the same row id), so by the effect-level rule school goes to ignore and its term stays in the formula. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance vi, which the formula leaves out. Konstantopoulos (2011), Research Synthesis Methods.
